paragraphs: Neural probabilistic language models can predict language well, but their training can be extremely slow. The paper identifies explicit normalization as a central bottleneck: computing the training gradients requires considering every word in the vocabulary. As the vocabulary grows, this makes each learning update expensive, even when the dataset itself is only moderately sized.

The proposed algorithm adapts noise-contrastive estimation to train these language models. This provides a way to estimate a model without the costly explicit normalization used in the usual training procedure. The authors also compare it with importance sampling, reporting greater efficiency and stability because good performance requires substantially fewer noise samples.

On the Penn Treebank corpus, the method cuts training time by more than an order of magnitude without reducing model quality. The authors also train models on 47 million words with an 80,000-word vocabulary and report state-of-the-art results on the Microsoft Research Sentence Completion Challenge. Together, these results support both the training method's efficiency and its usefulness at a larger scale.
icml-2012-a-fast-and-simple-algorithm-fo.tldr: Noise-contrastive estimation substantially speeds neural language-model training while preserving quality in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: For a robot to understand ordinary descriptions of its surroundings, words need to connect to things the robot can perceive. This paper studies that connection through grounded attribute learning: learning language meanings together with perceptual properties such as object color and shape. The motivation is to make interaction with robots more accessible to users without special training.

The approach jointly learns a perception model and a language model. Attribute classifiers provide the perceptual side, while a probabilistic categorial grammar supplies the language side. The grammar supports compositional meaning representations, so the model can build the meaning of a sentence from its parts rather than treating the entire sentence as an isolated label.

Evaluation focuses on sentences describing sets of objects in a physical workspace. The authors report accurate interpretation and effective induction of concepts represented by latent variables. These findings support the value of learning language and perception together: the model connects structured descriptions to properties of objects in grounded scenes.
icml-2012-a-joint-model-of-language-and-.tldr: A jointly learned language and perception model connects compositional object descriptions to attributes in physical scenes.

paragraphs: Sparse linear discriminant analysis seeks directions that distinguish classes while using relatively few input features. This paper introduces GLOSS, a method built on penalized optimal scoring. A central contribution is that its formulation retains an exact equivalence with sparse discriminant analysis, unlike the multiclass approaches based on regressing class indicators discussed in the abstract.

The optimization uses two nested convex problems. The main problem is a linear regression with a quadratic penalty that implements the group-lasso penalty. Group lasso selects a shared set of features across the discriminant directions, giving the model a compact overall feature set. The implementation also allows particular structure to be imposed on the within-class covariance matrix.

The authors report highly parsimonious models without compromising prediction performance, along with efficient computation for medium to large numbers of variables. The sparse directions also support low-dimensional representations of the data. These properties make the approach particularly relevant to gene expression analysis, where selecting a compact set of variables and representing class differences are both useful.
icml-2012-an-efficient-approach-to-spars.tldr: GLOSS efficiently formulates sparse discriminant analysis with shared feature selection across discriminant directions.

paragraphs: Marginal MAP inference in a graphical model combines finding a best assignment for selected variables with accounting for uncertainty in other variables. This paper introduces an anytime algorithm for that problem. The anytime design makes the amount of available computation central: the method supplies lower and upper bounds with guarantees under a fixed resource budget.

The authors analyze the algorithm's computational complexity and convergence rate, and relate it to earlier theoretical results. They show polynomial running time when the model's underlying graph has bounded tree-width. This is a structural condition on the graph, so the efficiency statement is tied to that condition rather than being an unrestricted claim about every graphical model.

Experiments use both real models and synthetically generated ones. The method compares favorably with Park and Darwiche's systematic search, especially on problems with many MAP variables and moderate tree-width. The contribution therefore combines a resource-aware inference procedure, theoretical analysis of its behavior, and empirical evidence identifying settings where it is particularly effective.
icml-2012-anytime-marginal-map-inference.tldr: An anytime marginal MAP algorithm provides guaranteed bounds under computational budgets and polynomial runtime for bounded-tree-width models.

paragraphs: Learning from an expert's demonstration becomes harder when an agent cannot fully observe its environment and does not know the environment's model. This paper studies how demonstrations can help estimate that model. Dialogue systems motivate the setting because explicitly specifying how the environment behaves can be difficult.

The key idea is to learn from the expert's choice of actions, as well as from the environment's reactions. The method infers the action-selection process behind a demonstration to extract information about model parameters. Its stated assumption is that the expert knows the true environment model and chooses optimal actions using that knowledge. Under this assumption, the choices themselves carry information about the environment.

The authors show that their algorithms can estimate model parameters from much shorter demonstrations than methods learning only from environmental reactions. The finding highlights an additional source of evidence in expert behavior: an action can reveal something about the model that made it optimal. The result depends on the stated interpretation of the expert's knowledge and decision-making.
icml-2012-apprenticeship-learning-for-mo.tldr: Assuming a knowledgeable, optimal expert, inferring why demonstration actions were chosen can reduce the data needed to learn an environment model.

paragraphs: Organizing high-dimensional data into a spatial tree involves a trade-off between the cost of choosing partitions and the quality of the resulting representation. This paper introduces approximate principal direction trees, which adapt to the data's intrinsic dimension. The aim is to approach the vector-quantization accuracy of PCA trees while retaining computational costs similar to random-projection trees.

At each recursive partition, the method uses a small number of power-method iterations to find a splitting plane. The number of iterations provides a way to trade running time for accuracy. Rather than requiring the full computation used for a principal direction, the method works with an approximation suited to constructing the tree.

The theory establishes strong performance guarantees regardless of the power method's convergence rate. It also shows that O(log d) iterations suffice to obtain the PCA-tree guarantee when intrinsic dimension is d. CPU and GPU demonstrations illustrate the trade-off and the data structure's effectiveness, connecting the theoretical argument to practical computation.
icml-2012-approximate-principal-directio.tldr: Approximate principal direction trees use a few power-method iterations to balance fast partitioning with PCA-like accuracy.

paragraphs: Hyperplane hashing searches quickly for data points near a hyperplane, a task useful for scaling active learning with support vector machines. Existing randomized approaches can require long codes and many hash tables to obtain reasonable accuracy. Those requirements increase memory use and reduce the speed advantage that hashing is intended to provide.

The paper proposes hash functions with a bilinear form to produce more compact codes. With random projections, these functions have higher collision probability than the existing hyperplane hash functions considered. The authors then introduce a framework that learns the bilinear functions directly from data, seeking codes that are both short and able to distinguish useful candidates.

Learning the functions improves search performance over the random-projection solutions reported in the paper. Large-scale active-learning experiments on two datasets, containing up to one million samples, demonstrate overall superiority of the proposed approach. The work links a change in hash-function design to practical improvements in the speed, storage, and search-quality trade-off.
icml-2012-compact-hyperplane-hashing-wit.tldr: Bilinear hyperplane hashing produces compact codes, with learned functions further improving search performance in large-scale active-learning experiments.

paragraphs: The Lasso regularization path describes how its fitted solution changes as the strength of regularization varies. Because this path is piecewise linear, algorithms can follow its successive straight segments and explicitly compute the entire path. This paper asks how expensive that apparently convenient strategy can become.

The authors prove that its worst-case complexity grows exponentially with the number of variables. Piecewise linearity therefore does not, by itself, ensure that computing every segment will be efficient. This is a worst-case result about the exact path, rather than a statement that every dataset produces an exponentially difficult computation.

The paper then establishes a more favorable result for approximation. An approximate path can always be obtained with at most O(1/√ε) linear segments, with every point satisfying a relative ε-duality-gap guarantee. This gives a quantitative connection between approximation tolerance and path size. A practical algorithm accompanies the theory, making the contribution both a warning about exact path-following and a constructive approach to controlled approximation.
icml-2012-complexity-analysis-of-the-las.tldr: Exact Lasso paths can have exponential worst-case complexity, while approximate paths admit a bounded number of segments with explicit accuracy guarantees.

paragraphs: In a sensor network, observations and computing resources are spread across multiple nodes. Estimating a statistical model therefore calls for methods that can work with this distribution of data and computation. The paper proposes a general approach based on combining local estimates constructed from components of the pseudo-likelihood.

The framework includes several ways to combine those estimates, rather than prescribing a single costly joint optimization. Its central finding is that simple linear combinations or max-voting methods can be statistically competitive with more advanced joint optimization when they incorporate second-order information. That qualification matters: the claim concerns these simple methods equipped with additional statistical information.

The authors provide both theoretical and experimental analysis. They also emphasize low communication and computation costs, along with anytime behavior that allows the algorithms to produce results during their operation. These properties make the approach relevant when coordination itself is expensive. The contribution is evidence that carefully combining local estimators can retain strong statistical performance without requiring the full expense of joint optimization.
icml-2012-distributed-parameter-estimati.tldr: Combining local pseudo-likelihood estimators with second-order information can compete statistically with costlier joint optimization.

paragraphs: The Hessian describes a function's second-order behavior, but obtaining it can be computationally expensive. This paper develops Curvature Propagation, a general method for estimating the Hessian of a function represented by a computational graph. Its estimates are unbiased, meaning that their average targets the Hessian rather than a systematically shifted quantity.

At roughly the cost of two gradient evaluations, the method produces a rank-one approximation of the entire Hessian. Repeating the procedure provides increasingly precise estimates of selected entries or of the whole matrix. The diagonal receives particular attention because the abstract identifies a lack of a general method that is both efficient and accurate for computing it.

Experiments report accurate neural-network Hessian estimates with relatively little computation. The authors also apply the method to score matching, whose objective directly involves a Hessian diagonal. In that setting, exact computation commonly uses inefficient algorithms that scale poorly to larger models. Curvature Propagation offers an estimation-based route for handling that expensive part of the objective.
icml-2012-estimating-the-hessian-by-back.tldr: Curvature Propagation efficiently produces unbiased Hessian estimates that become more precise with repeated computation.

paragraphs: Strong visual object detectors combine sophisticated features, discriminative classifiers, and large amounts of data for finding difficult negative examples. Their success is often attributed to a classifier's ability to generalize across different positive examples of an object category. This paper examines that explanation through a deliberately simple alternative.

Instead of learning one classifier from multiple positive instances, the authors train a separate classifier for each positive object instance. Each individual classifier therefore cannot learn commonality across positive training instances. This changes a central part of the usual category-based setup and makes it possible to examine whether combining positive examples within a classifier is essential to the observed performance.

The experiments show no drastic performance drop relative to standard category-based approaches. That finding challenges the idea that generalization across positive instances must be the main reason such detectors work well. The authors frame the conclusion cautiously: the results suggest that the conventional explanation may not necessarily hold, rather than proving that shared category-level learning is never useful.
icml-2012-exemplar-svms-for-visual-ob-je.tldr: Training one classifier per positive instance caused no drastic detection-performance drop, questioning a common explanation of category-based detectors' success.

paragraphs: Statistical leverage scores describe structural nonuniformity among a matrix's rows, and coherence is the largest of these scores. They are defined using squared row lengths in a matrix of left singular vectors. These quantities matter in matrix completion, low-rank approximation, and randomized matrix algorithms, where uneven row contributions affect how computation should be organized.

The paper gives a randomized algorithm that approximates every leverage score with relative error for an arbitrary n-by-d matrix with many more rows than columns. Its running time is O(nd log n), compared with O(nd²) for the straightforward method based on computing an orthogonal basis for the matrix's range.

The construction carefully applies random projections on both sides of the input matrix. The result resolves a previously open question and immediately improves methods for coreset-based least-squares regression, coherence estimation, and related low-rank matrix problems. Its significance is that useful structural information about a large matrix can be approximated without paying the full cost of the direct basis computation.
icml-2012-fast-approximation-of-matrix-c.tldr: A randomized algorithm approximates all leverage scores of a tall matrix in O(nd log n) time instead of the naive O(nd²).

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups data according to underlying subspaces. A common reconstruction-based approach first represents data points using other points, converts the resulting reconstruction matrix into pairwise affinities, and then applies spectral clustering. The paper argues that the success of such methods relies heavily on subspace independence, which may fail in applications such as face clustering as the number of groups increases.

The proposed method retains reconstruction as its starting point but does not make the subspace independence assumption. It explicitly expresses properties of the reconstruction matrix through latent cluster indicators: variables representing cluster memberships that must be inferred. This connects the reconstruction model directly to the grouping the method is trying to discover.

The affinity matrix for spectral clustering is built from the posterior distribution of those indicators. Thus, inferred cluster membership informs the similarities used in the final clustering stage. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the approach can outperform state-of-the-art alternatives, supporting the usefulness of this formulation without claiming superiority on every dataset.
icml-2012-groupwise-constrained-reconstr.tldr: Latent cluster indicators guide reconstruction-based subspace clustering without assuming independent subspaces.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate high-dimensional undirected graphical models while combining modeling flexibility with robustness. The proposed method, nonparanormal SKEPTIC, uses Gaussian copula graphical models. This supplies a more flexible modeling framework than a standard Gaussian graphical model while retaining a structure suitable for estimating relationships among many variables.

For robust estimation, the method uses rank-based correlation estimates, including Spearman's rho and Kendall's tau. The theoretical result is that it achieves the optimal parametric convergence rate for both graph estimation and parameter estimation in high-dimensional settings. Thus, the additional modeling flexibility does not prevent the stated optimal rate from being attained.

The authors interpret this result as suggesting that Gaussian copula models can safely replace Gaussian graphical models, even for genuinely Gaussian data. They also compare graph recovery through numerical simulations under ideal and noisy conditions, then apply the methods to a large genomic dataset. These studies complement the convergence analysis with evidence of empirical usefulness, rather than turning the theoretical rate into a universal claim about every finite dataset.
icml-2012-high-dimensional-semiparametri.tldr: Nonparanormal SKEPTIC combines rank-based robustness with Gaussian copula flexibility while achieving optimal parametric convergence rates.

paragraphs: Image-labeling systems often lack enough labeled training data. This paper explores using existing maps to supply labels for aerial images. Maps offer abundant supervision, but their information may be incomplete or poorly aligned with the images. A mapped feature can therefore supply an imperfect training target even when the map is useful overall.

The authors propose two robust loss functions designed to address these kinds of label noise. A loss function determines how prediction errors influence training, so changing it changes how the learning process responds to unreliable supervision. The proposed losses are used to train a deep neural network on two challenging aerial-image datasets.

The reported experiments show large performance improvements from the robust losses, and the best system substantially exceeds the best published results for the task considered. The contribution is a way to make abundant but imperfect map labels more useful for learning. The evidence specifically concerns the incomplete and misregistered labels addressed in these aerial-image experiments.
icml-2012-learning-to-label-aerial-image.tldr: Two robust training losses help deep networks learn aerial-image labels from incomplete and misaligned maps.

paragraphs: A Markov decision process can be difficult to control when its parameters are uncertain. The paper argues that treating uncertainty at different states as uncoupled leads to conservative solutions. Such a treatment does not connect the uncertain behavior encountered at one state with what can happen elsewhere in the decision process.

The proposed alternative couples uncertainty by limiting how many times the system may deviate from its nominal parameters. This is the precise modeling idea behind the title's lightning metaphor. The restriction places a shared bound on deviations, allowing the control problem to represent uncertainty that is constrained across the process rather than handled independently at each state.

The authors provide probabilistic guarantees supporting the model's relevance to real-life situations and develop tractable algorithms for computing optimal control policies within it. The resulting policies are optimal for this bounded-deviation formulation. The contribution combines a different representation of parameter uncertainty with algorithms that make the representation computationally usable.
icml-2012-lightning-does-not-strike-twic.tldr: Bounding the number of parameter deviations couples uncertainty across an MDP and enables tractable optimal-policy computation.

paragraphs: Related regression tasks can benefit from shared information, but they need not use exactly the same variables. This paper introduces Multi-level Lasso to select variables across tasks while allowing their sparsity patterns to differ. The aim is to use common structure without forcing every task to have an identical set of nonzero coefficients.

The method expresses regression coefficients as a product of two components. One component is shared by all tasks, while the other captures task-specific behavior. This decomposition produces an objective that can be solved efficiently through alternating optimization. It gives shared and individual structure explicit roles in determining the fitted coefficients.

The authors analyze the special case of an orthonormal design to explain how the method shrinks coefficients compared with related approaches. They also provide theoretical consistency guarantees and evaluate the framework through simulations and a microarray-data study. Together, these contributions support a flexible approach to sparse multitask regression, with both mathematical analysis and empirical evidence for its value.
icml-2012-multi-level-lasso-for-sparse-m.tldr: Multi-level Lasso multiplies shared and task-specific coefficient components to select variables flexibly across related regression tasks.

paragraphs: Learning features from multiple observations can require representing how images relate, rather than only what each image contains. This paper examines that problem for settings such as image sequences and binocular observations. It focuses on the role of multiplying filter responses or applying squaring nonlinearities in sparse-coding models that learn image relationships.

The analysis shows that training these models amounts to jointly diagonalizing matrices that encode image transformations. Inference, in turn, corresponds to detecting rotations within shared eigenspaces. This gives a mathematical interpretation of the learned representation: the multiplicative or squared responses are connected to the structure of transformations between images.

The framework helps explain earlier experimental observations that Fourier features and circular Fourier features emerge when complex-cell models are trained on translating or rotating images. It also shows how learning transformations can make it possible to learn invariant features. The contribution is an explanatory link between model operations, transformation structure, and representations that can remain stable under changes to an image.
icml-2012-on-multi-view-feature-learning.tldr: The paper connects multiplicative multi-view feature learning to joint matrix diagonalization and transformation-dependent rotations in shared eigenspaces.

paragraphs: Many classification applications need a probability of class membership, rather than just a predicted class. This paper proposes obtaining such probabilities through a two-stage procedure. First, it optimizes a ranking loss; then, it applies isotonic regression to turn the resulting scores into probability predictions.

The stages address related but distinct requirements. Ranking concerns how examples are ordered, while probability prediction also concerns the numerical values attached to those examples. Isotonic regression supplies an order-preserving fit for that second stage. The paper presents the combination as a simple semiparametric technique that offers both good ranking and good regression performance.

The authors state that the approach can model a richer collection of probability distributions than logistic regression and support its usefulness with experiments on real-world probability-prediction applications. The result shows how an objective aimed at ranking can form part of a probability-estimation method when followed by a suitable fitting step. Its reported effectiveness belongs to the combined procedure, not merely to ranking scores on their own.
icml-2012-predicting-accurate-probabilit.tldr: Optimizing a ranking loss and then applying isotonic regression yields flexible probability predictions with good reported ranking and regression performance.

paragraphs: Some classification data form a graph, such as webpages joined by hyperlinks. Collective classification uses these connections alongside information about individual examples. Although this can improve accuracy, many methods expect a fully labeled training graph. This paper addresses the more common situation in which only a small portion of the graph has labels.

The authors combine classifiers to take advantage of differences between relational features, which describe connections, and non-relational features, which describe instances themselves. They also extend label regularization to these hybrid classifiers. This lets unlabeled data influence the learning process, giving the model information beyond the small set of directly labeled examples.

Experiments show significant accuracy increases on three real datasets, and the techniques are described as efficient and easy to implement. The results also help explain conflicting conclusions in earlier related studies. The contribution is therefore both practical and interpretive: it offers a way to learn collective classifiers from sparse labels while clarifying how choices in the learning approach can matter.
icml-2012-semi-supervised-collective-cla.tldr: Hybrid classifiers and label regularization improve collective classification when only a small fraction of a data graph is labeled.

paragraphs: Bayesian topic models need inference methods that remain practical as both text collections and the number of topics grow. This paper introduces a hybrid algorithm for latent Dirichlet allocation that combines two useful properties: the efficiency of sparse Gibbs sampling and the scalability of online stochastic inference. The contribution centers on bringing those properties into one inference method.

The reported scale is substantial: the algorithm handles 1.2 million books containing 33 billion words, with thousands of topics, on one CPU. This result demonstrates that the combined approach can operate on a very large corpus without requiring multiple CPUs in the reported application. It also addresses a setting with a large topic collection, not merely a large amount of text.

The authors state that the method reduces variational-inference bias and extends to many Bayesian models with hidden variables. The broader significance is a combination of scalable computation and improved inference behavior. The claim is a reduction in bias, rather than its complete elimination, and generalization to many such models rather than every Bayesian model.
icml-2012-sparse-stochastic-inference-fo.tldr: Combining sparse Gibbs sampling with online stochastic inference scales topic modeling to 33 billion words on one CPU while reducing variational bias.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs such as trees, graphs, and sequences. Fully annotating these outputs can be tedious or infeasible when they are large. This paper introduces a large-margin formulation that allows learning from partial annotations, so training does not require every structural detail to be specified.

The resulting optimization problem is nonconvex. The authors solve it using the concave-convex procedure, together with new strategies that speed up computation. They also provide a unifying view of earlier structured-learning approaches based on hinge, ramp, and max losses, followed by an empirical comparison of how those losses perform in practice.

The application is a challenging tracking-by-assignment task involving a variable number of objects that can divide. On this benchmark, using only 25% of a full annotation produces performance comparable to training with complete annotation. This is evidence that substantial annotation savings are possible in the tested setting. The central contribution is a learning formulation that can make incomplete structural supervision useful, supported by both optimization work and a concrete tracking result.
icml-2012-structured-learning-from-parti.tldr: A large-margin method learns structured outputs from partial annotations, matching full-annotation performance with 25% annotation on a tracking benchmark.

paragraphs: Total variation and Euler's elastica have been useful for image-processing tasks such as denoising and filling missing regions. This paper investigates how to bring these forms of smoothing into supervised learning on high-dimensional data. It frames learning as minimizing an energy that combines squared prediction loss with one of the two smoothing terms.

The formulation follows a Tikhonov regularization scheme, balancing agreement with training targets against the chosen smoothing requirement. Applying variational principles leads to an Euler–Lagrange partial differential equation. However, the equation is high-dimensional and cannot be directly handled by common solution methods, creating a computational obstacle to using the formulation.

The authors address that obstacle by approximating the target function with radial basis functions. This turns the task into finding the basis functions' linear coefficients. They evaluate the resulting methods on binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression benchmarks, reporting promising experimental results. The contribution is both an extension of these smoothing ideas to supervised learning and a workable approximation for the resulting high-dimensional problem.
icml-2012-total-variation-and-euler-s-el.tldr: Radial basis approximations make total-variation and Euler's-elastica regularization usable for high-dimensional supervised learning.

paragraphs: When several judges rate the same items, their ratings can be used both to estimate the true labels and to understand the judges themselves. This paper emphasizes the second purpose: gaining diagnostic insight into trained, in-house judges. That focus shifts attention toward what disagreements reveal about individual rating behavior.

The authors generalize the Dawid–Skene model into a family of probabilistic models organized around true labels and confusion. This framework connects an item's underlying label with the labels that judges assign, making their patterns of confusion part of the analysis. Within the family, the authors propose a hierarchical Bayesian model called HybridConfusion.

HybridConfusion consistently outperforms Dawid–Skene on the synthetic and real-world datasets reported. The result supports the proposed model within those evaluations, while the broader modeling framework offers multiple ways to analyze ratings under a shared perspective. The contribution matters because aggregating ratings need not end with a single inferred answer: the same modeling problem can also support understanding how trained judges differ.
icml-2012-truelabel-confusions-a-spectru.tldr: HybridConfusion extends true-label-and-confusion modeling to analyze trained judges and outperforms Dawid–Skene on the reported datasets.

paragraphs: Efficient neural-network applications can require substantial systems expertise, especially as datasets grow. This paper argues that general-purpose compilers miss optimization opportunities available from knowledge of neural networks. It focuses on a specific property: when a network's architecture remains fixed during training, its underlying data structure can be optimized ahead of time.

The authors introduce SONNC, a neural-network compiler that uses static analysis to generate optimized parallel code. The compiler uses architectural information that is already known before training to specialize the implementation. This places some of the burden of producing efficient code in the compilation process rather than requiring researchers to manage every optimization themselves.

The reported experiments show speedups of up to 242 times over optimized MATLAB code. SONNC also significantly reduces code complexity for structurally sparse networks. The speedup is a reported maximum, not a uniform improvement across all applications. Together, the findings demonstrate the potential of architecture-aware compilation to improve execution speed and simplify the implementation of sparse neural networks.
icml-2012-utilizing-static-analysis-and-.tldr: SONNC uses fixed network architecture to generate optimized parallel code, reporting up to 242-fold speedups over optimized MATLAB.
